To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified genetic contributions to inflammatory biomarkers (CRP) and hemostatic markers (fibrinogen) in a stroke population, and that these genetic contributions were also associated with risk for ischemic stroke and for recurrent stroke.

we identified novel associations of CRP with AKR1D, and of fibrinogen level with LEPR, and that we found shared genetic susceptibility of vascular risk biomarkers with recurrent stroke and specific stroke subtypes.
(1) we discovered an association between CRPs and CRP single nucleotides polymorphisms (most associated SNP rs2592902 p = 1,14×10−9) circulating CRP levels in 2100 VISP participants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic contributors to circulating biomarkers and ischemic stroke.
the genetic contributors to vascular-related biomarkers and their association with stroke and stroke subtypes.
identifying genetic contributors to biomarkers and risk of ischemic and recurrent strokes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic contributors to vascular-related biomarkers are shared with ischemic and other recurrent stroke.
the genetic contribution to circulating CRP level is associated with ischemic stroke risk.
the genetic contributors to biomarkers of ischemia and recurrent stroke are not yet well established and that further research in this field is warranted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic contribution to CRP is associated with ischemic stroke risk and the genetic contribution to fibrinogen is not associated with stroke.
there is a shared genetic contribution to vascular biomarkers and ischemic stroke.
there is a shared genetic susceptibility for CRP, fibrinogen, and ischemic stroke.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic variants in the CRP gene and in the gene AKR1D, a regulator of CRP expression, are associated with circulating levels of CRP.
the genetic contributors to circulating biomarker levels and stroke risk are not identical.
there is a strong genetic basis for circulating levels of inflammatory markers, and that these genetic factors may also be involved in the risk for stroke.
